Read the rent band behind a vacancy headline

Four charts follow Canadian purpose-built rental vacancy rates across rent quartiles, compare percentage-point changes and keep market availability separate from a household housing budget.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

The central idea

A vacancy percentage describes units within a defined rental market and snapshot. It does not identify how many homes meet a household’s price, location and timing requirements.

01

A rental-market headline can hide a different picture across rent bands

In CMHC’s 2025 national rent-quartile figure, the lowest-rent quartile has a 1.4% vacancy rate, while the highest-rent quartile has a 5.3% rate. Both describe purpose-built rental apartments, but they do not describe the same price segment.

A prospective tenant with a limited budget therefore needs more than a broad statement that vacancies increased. More unoccupied higher-rent units do not automatically create options at a lower household price limit.

The charts adapt the accessible data table for Figure 2 of CMHC’s 2025 Rental Market Report. They preserve all 44 values from 2015 through 2025 in one source vintage. The report was released on 11 December 2025 and reviewed here on 25 October 2026.

02

Vacancy describes a unit’s status at the survey point

CMHC’s survey methodology defines a vacant unit as physically unoccupied and available for immediate rental at the survey. The annual Rental Market Survey is conducted in October, so its results describe that snapshot.

The survey targets privately initiated rental structures with at least three units that have been on the market for at least three months. Its frame excludes social and affordable housing structures or units. The figure used here is specifically the purpose-built apartment series, rather than the separate condominium-rental market.

Vacancy is not a household acceptance rate. It also does not count every unit that may become available after a tenant gives notice, every advertised property or every home a reader could realistically rent. Those populations and timing questions need their own evidence.

03

Q1 through Q4 are rent ranks, not calendar quarters

The source labels its four groups Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q4. Here they mean rent quartiles, ordered from the lowest-rent to the highest-rent band. The eleven annual rows are 2015 through 2025.

Reading “Q1 2025” as a January-to-March observation would confuse two different dimensions. The charts instead spell out Lowest, Second, Third and Highest rent quartile and label survey years separately.

The accessible figure provides rates without the underlying rent cutoffs or band-specific unit counts. This page does not invent a CAD boundary for any quartile, equate the lowest band with a reader’s budget or assign the reader to an income group from a rent rank.

04

Separate percentage-point increases from relative rate changes

Between the displayed 2024 and 2025 snapshots, the lowest-rent rate rises from 0.7% to 1.4%. That is a 0.7-percentage-point increase. Relative to its original 0.7% level, the rate doubles, giving a 100% relative increase.

The other source bands move from 1.2% to 2.3%, from 2.0% to 3.1%, and from 4.5% to 5.3%. Their percentage-point changes are +1.1, +1.1 and +0.8 respectively.

The lowest band’s rate can therefore double while remaining much lower than the highest band’s rate. A relative increase and a final level answer different questions. The signed change chart displays percentage points and makes no claim that the observed differences are statistically significant.

05

The historical ordering is not a permanent rule

The selected lowest-rent series is not always the band with the lowest vacancy. In the source’s 2015 snapshot, its rate is 4.8%, above the highest-rent band’s 2.9%. By 2025 the ordering is reversed.

The line and matrix keep that history visible. They do not fit a trend or imply that a particular property stayed in the same quartile throughout the period. Rental stock, rent-band membership and market conditions can change between snapshots.

The report also notes a 2025 methodological update for assigning units with unknown bedroom counts. This page keeps the report’s published overall rent-quartile figure and creates no bedroom-specific history. A more detailed comparison would need the relevant definitions, unit counts and source tables.

06

A rate inside a band is not that band’s share of all vacancies

A 1.4% vacancy rate in a rent band means a vacancy estimate relative to the stock in that band. It does not mean that 1.4% of all vacant apartments belong to the band.

To turn rates into numbers of vacancies, the corresponding unit denominators are needed. To combine rates into an overall market measure, the appropriate source weights and coverage are needed. The figure’s percentages alone do not supply them.

The page therefore does not average the four rounded rates and label the result Canada’s overall vacancy rate. It also does not multiply a national band rate by a local listing count or by the number of a household’s applications.

07

Price the complete housing option against actual household cash

Consider a separate original budget illustration: monthly take-home cash is CAD 4,500, other expenses are CAD 1,800 and planned saving is CAD 500. That leaves CAD 2,200 for the housing costs included in the comparison.

An independently chosen option with CAD 2,000 rent, CAD 150 utilities, CAD 100 parking and CAD 30 tenant insurance totals CAD 2,280. Its CAD 80 monthly gap does not disappear because an aggregate vacancy rate rose.

These selected amounts are not CMHC observations or a claim about a particular rent quartile. Their purpose is to show the household calculation that the market statistic cannot perform. Moving costs, deposits, overlapping rent and receipt dates need a separate cash calendar.

08

Use market context to sharpen the search and the cash plan

The four source charts describe historical vacancy rates across rent bands. A household decision also depends on current quotes, included services, location, bedrooms, accessibility, lease timing and the cash available before a move.

CMHC’s rent methodology notes that utilities and services may be included or excluded in reported rent. Confirming those details for an actual option helps avoid comparing a rent-only number with a complete housing budget.

  1. Read the market, dwelling type and survey date.
  2. Check whether Q1–Q4 describe rent ranks or calendar quarters.
  3. Distinguish a rate, a rate change and a count of vacant units.
  4. Obtain current options matching the household’s requirements.
  5. Budget the full monthly cost and the upfront payment calendar.

The historical selectors leave the original observations intact. They help compare source views and do not predict the time, price or outcome of a reader’s next rental search.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. 44 public CMHC estimates from national Figure 2 of the 2025 Rental Market Report, covering rent quartiles for 2015–2025. Rates, differences and historical selections are descriptive. No personal search probability, rent threshold or forecast is estimated. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.
